newsitem.title: TANZANIA: FOCUS -- Tanzania coffee industry set for shake-up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS -- Tanzania coffee industry set for shake-up.

text.p: Tanzania's second annual coffee industry conference, ended Wednesday, was mostly taken up with debate on how to revitalise the country's coffee industry, its biggest foreign exchange earner.
The conference was attended by 160 participants, representing all sectors of the coffee industry.

They heard how drought, outmoded farming practices, high taxes and levies, input supply, disease, poor plant husbandry, ageing trees, inadequate infrastructure, and loss of farmer interest, were all key factors for declining output in an increasingly competitive world coffee market.
Infrastructure in rural Tanzania remains in a poor state of repair -- especially electricity, roads and telecommunications -- posing a major threat to investment.
Agricultual and Cooperatives Minister Paul Kimiti said major issues such as poor or non-existent input supplies to farmers had to be solved.
Kimiti said an European Union-funded compensation scheme worth ECU 11 million should act as an incentive "to push farmers to raise production and invest seriously in their coffee crop."

A severe drought affecting much of East Africa has wiped out prospects for a recovery in Tanzania's coffee production for the 1997/98 season. Worst affected areas include the premium mild washed arabica zones of the foothills of Mount Kilimanjaro.
From a peak production averaging 55,160 tonnes in 1981 to 1985, output has slumped in recent years and is projected at 41,000 tonnes in 1996/97 season worth about $95 million.
Kimiti said replanting of Tanzania's ageing coffee trees should be treated as a matter of urgency and noted that seedling production for 1996/97 totalled more than three million plants.
Distribution would start in the coming 1997/98 season. Under EU funding, contract growers would receive 50 shillings (83 U.S. cents) for every seedling grown and distributed to farmers.
The initiative aimed to encourage the development of coffee nurseries as a private activity, Kimiti said.
More farmer education was required especially on the use of fertilisers although growers complained that with declining income from lowered output, the cost burden was untenable.

"If we have learned one lesson from the the last few years, it is, that farmers are under-utilising inputs which has led to a substantial decrease in production. The issue of inputs to this industry is a matter of life and death," Kimiti said.
Land usage emerged as a key factor affecting production.

Tanzania Coffee Board (TCB) Managing Director Edward Sannda called for the doubling in size of peasant holdings from a current average of half a hectare, saying anything less was not economically viable.
Kimiti called on coffee researchers "to make every effort" to provide improved varieties to farmers as soon as possible.
Traders complained about taxes and levies and expressed grave concern about the possible imposition in 1998 of a Value Added Tax (VAT) on coffee exports.

TCB officials said Tanzania would step up promotion of Tanzanian coffee and would in April attend an exhibition sponsored by the Speciality Coffee Association of America in New Orleans where neighbours Kenya and Uganda would also be present.
In the same month, the TCB's marketing roadshow would move to Japan for the Tokyo International Trade Fair.
